premise: A humorous animated timeline detailing a gamer's frustratingly long, 13-year wait for the release of Grand Theft Auto 6.

hook.first_2s_visual: A split screen showing a young gamer in a bright room on the left, and an older, tired version of the same gamer in a dark room on the right.
hook.first_line_technique: It immediately establishes a massive time jump and a relatable premise (waiting for a highly anticipated game).

structure.what_happens: Introduces Jake at 17 waiting for GTA 6, and reveals he'll be 30 when he finally plays it.
structure.why_it_works: Sets the stakes and the comedic premise of the extreme wait.

structure.what_happens: Explains how the massive success of GTA 5 and GTA Online caused Rockstar to delay a sequel.
structure.why_it_works: Uses facts and relatable gamer behavior to explain the delay.

structure.what_happens: The year Jake expected GTA 6, Rockstar releases Red Dead Redemption 2 instead.
structure.why_it_works: Adds another layer of delay, though a welcome one, extending the timeline.

structure.what_happens: More years pass, GTA 5 is re-released again, GTA 6 is finally announced but suffers multiple release date pushbacks.
structure.why_it_works: Builds frustration and highlights the absurdity of the wait.

structure.what_happens: Present day: Jake is 30, a father, and finally has the game pre-loaded.
structure.why_it_works: Resolves the initial setup, showing the passage of time in his personal life.

structure.what_happens: A scary thought: if GTA 7 takes another 13 years, Jake will be 43 and his kid will be 13, starting the cycle over.
structure.why_it_works: Ends on a funny, slightly depressing realization that loops back to the beginning.

shots.subject: Split screen of young Jake (day) and older Jake (night) sitting on a beanbag/couch playing games.
The screen wipes to show only young Jake in his bright room in 2013.
A pan across a shelf showing the relatively quick release schedule of previous GTA games.
Back to young Jake on his beanbag.
A time-lapse wipe changes Jake's appearance (older, different clothes) and his room setup (better chair, new console).
Another wipe shows Jake even older, wearing a tie, sitting on a proper couch in a new apartment.
A wipe to the present day, Jake in a hoodie in a dark room, looking tired.
A wipe back to the original young Jake in 2013.

pacing.where_it_slows_down: During the explanation of Red Dead Redemption 2's development taking up all resources.
pacing.where_it_speeds_up: When listing the rapid succession of GTA 6 release date delays.

look.palette: Bright, flat colors for the past, transitioning to cooler, darker tones for the present.
look.lighting: Flat and even, except for the final scene which uses the glow of the TV screen to light the character.
look.character_design: Simple, meme-inspired 'sock puppet' style characters with minimal facial features but expressive accessories (hair, hats, clothes).

voice.tone: Wry, narrative, slightly cynical but relatable.
voice.energy_curve: Starts steady, builds slight frustration during the delays, ends on a contemplative, humorous note.
voice.delivery_tricks: Uses pauses effectively before delivering punchlines or revealing new delays.

music.where_it_drops: No major drops, it serves as a continuous, chill background track.
music.how_it_supports_the_story: The relaxed, repetitive nature of the beat contrasts humorously with the frustrating, decades-long wait being described.

sfx: Subtle 'pop' sounds when new items (consoles, games, money) appear on screen; cash register 'cha-ching' for GTA 5's success; 'whoosh' sounds for the time-lapse wipes.
hero_moments: The final sequence where the narrator calculates the wait for GTA 7, and an older, grey-haired Jake appears next to the young Jake, visually representing the cyclical nature of the wait.
captions: Center-screen, dynamic, popping in word-by-word or in short phrases, white text with a thick black outline for readability.
why_it_works: Taps into a universally understood frustration within the gaming community.
Uses a single character's aging process to visually represent the passage of time.
The simple animation style allows for quick visual gags and easy transitions.
The script is tight, moving quickly through a 13-year timeline without getting bogged down.
The ending provides a clever, cyclical punchline that rewards the viewer.
rules_to_borrow: Use a split-screen 'before and after' in the first 3 seconds to establish the core conflict.
Visually represent the passage of time by changing the character's clothes, environment, or accessories rather than just stating the year.
Use pop-up graphics (like the money raining or the tweets) to illustrate data points without breaking the visual style.
If telling a chronological story, use a consistent transition effect (like the vertical wipe) to signify time jumps.
End with a 'scary thought' or a projection into the future to leave the audience with a lingering idea.
Keep the background music consistent if the story spans a long time, to provide a sense of continuity.
do_not_copy: The specific 'Flork' character design (white blob with simple face).
The exact timeline of GTA releases.
